source.title: LLM Layers Immediately Correct Each Other
source.authors: Arjun Patrawala; Jiahai Feng; Erik Jones; Jacob Steinhardt

page_placements.theme: Counterbalancing in ordinary forward passes: later components partly cancel or damp earlier writes and confident predictions, with no ablation
Graded, dose-dependent counter-response: downstream responses scale with the upstream write, so removing the write looks like compensation

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some figure and table content is flattened from PDF extraction, but the relevant text descriptions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies ordinary adjacent-layer correction (TLCM), not the effect of ablating a component on the final prediction. It distinguishes TLCM from ablation-triggered self-repair and does not test the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior self-repair work but reports no ablation experiment measuring restoration of the original prediction or comparing an ablation's total output effect with its direct effect. Its own measurements concern adjacent-layer contribution similarities, responses to scaling a prior-layer contribution, and Jacobian structure; these are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study measures adjacent-layer anticorrelation (TLCM) during ordinary forward passes. It never ablates a component to measure restoration of the output or prediction. It cites self-repair and explicitly separates TLCM from it. The one compensation-like result, layer i+1 boosting layer i's direction when layer i's contribution is removed from its input (α = −1), is measured as a cosine similarity, not as output recovery. The authors also say it may stem from mechanisms unrelated to TLCM. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that adjacent layers in 5 of 7 families systematically counteract parts of each other's contributions during ordinary inference. They add that this emerges in pretraining, is adaptive and selective by subspace, and is distinct from ablation-triggered self-repair. Propose-and-reject is offered as an untested interpretation.
record.recipe_differences: The original studies investigate self-repair following component ablation. This paper measures ordinary adjacent-layer contribution similarities, perturbs a later layer's input by scaling the prior-layer contribution, and analyzes layer Jacobians; it does not ablate components or measure restoration of the model's prediction.
record.method_sensitivity: TLCM is reported in 5 of 7 model families and absent in GPT-2 and Phi; it is strongest in the first two-thirds of layers. Its activation frequency differs by token type and increases with context position. The α = −1 compensation response is strongest in earlier layers.

fits_no_version.finding: In 5 of 7 model families, adjacent layers write anticorrelated residual contributions in ordinary forward passes (cosine about −0.2, as low as −0.4). This is absent in GPT-2 and Phi; non-adjacent layers are orthogonal or positive.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adjacent transformer layers partially reverse each other's contributions without any ablation.

fits_no_version.finding: Layer i+1's opposing response scales roughly linearly with layer i's contribution. At α = −1 it flips to boosting layer i's direction, strongest in earlier layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The next layer adaptively adjusts to the prior layer's contribution, including compensation when that contribution is removed from its input.

fits_no_version.finding: Jacobian eigen-analysis shows selective correction (mode near λ = −1) and reinforcement (near 0.5) in TLCM pairs, versus a peak at 0 for non-TLCM pairs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In TLCM-active pairs, the next layer selectively cancels some subspaces of the prior contribution and reinforces others.

fits_no_version.finding: Attention sublayers correlate positively with each other, while MLPs anticorrelate with prior MLP and attention outputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MLPs carry most of adjacent-layer correction.

fits_no_version.finding: TLCM activation counts vary by token: higher on numbers, punctuation and dates, lower on common words, and near zero on BOS.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ordinary forward-pass layer correction is token-dependent.

record.problems: The experiments do not measure the claim's ablation-to-output-restoration effect. The paper notes that α = −1 is counterfactual and may involve mechanisms unrelated to TLCM; Jacobian analysis is a local linearization. Many layer-similarity and sublayer results are presented qualitatively or in figures, and numerical uncertainty is not provided for most of those measurements.

untested.parts: No attention-layer ablation followed by measurement of later attention layers restoring the output.
No measurement of late-MLP effects on the maximum-likelihood token or of change under upstream ablation. MLP anticorrelation (R9) concerns adjacent-layer contributions, not logits.
No single-head ablations and no compensation measure on general text.
No measure of ablation-induced compensation, its variance across prompts, or overcorrection.
No backup heads, copy-suppression heads, LayerNorm rescaling or anti-erasure neurons studied. Appendix A discusses RMSNorm as a cause of TLCM, not of self-repair.
No comparison of zero ablation with mean or resample ablation.

record.verdict_notes: Several results have no row: emergence over training (Section 4.2, OLMo checkpoints), the position effect (Figure 2) and saturation at α > 2 (Appendix F.2). They bear on no version, so they are not listed as missing. The record's code_released URL is given in the paper, but the checklist says code was not released.

versions.untested_parts: No layer ablation followed by measurement of later attention layers restoring the output or prediction.
No measurement of late MLP effects on the maximum-likelihood token, or of how that effect changes when earlier components are ablated.
No single-head ablations or full-distribution measurements across general text, model families, or sizes.
The paper does not measure ablation-induced compensation by prompt, its variability, or overcorrection relative to an ablation's output effect.
The paper studies layer-level Jacobian subspaces and sublayer correlations, not the named mechanisms in this version.
No on-distribution ablation comparison (mean, resample, or otherwise) against zero ablation.
No measurement of how ablation-based importance scores compare with a component's function or effect.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Set α = −1 in the perturbation to the input of layer i+1

conditions.value: effect occurs most strongly in earlier layers

rows.measure: Cosine similarity between adjacent layer contributions after perturbation
rows.value: Cosine similarity becomes positive; layer i+1 effectively boosts layer i's contribution
rows.note: The authors caution that α = −1 is a counterfactual state and that this compensation may arise from mechanisms unrelated to TLCM.
rows.check: This is the closest row to V1. Removing layer i's contribution from layer i+1's input makes their cosine positive. But it involves whole layers (attention+MLP), measures direction rather than restoration of the output, and the authors flag it as counterfactual and possibly unrelated. Keep it unlinked; the 'observed' state refers only to the cosine flip, not to self-repair.

relation.reason: The paper discusses self-repair as related work and a possible explanation for counterfactual compensation, while distinguishing it from ordinary-forward-pass TLCM.

tranche.reason: TLCM measures residual-contribution anticorrelation and its response to scaling, rather than any defined claim version. The alpha = -1 experiment measures directional compensation by a whole transformer layer, without attention-layer isolation or output-restoration measurement.

source_check.notes: The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate. R4/R5 use a scaling intervention that retains the preceding residual stream; the paper cautions that extreme-alpha compensation may involve self-repair mechanisms unrelated to TLCM.
